transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well, I came in because I just… I can’t seem to settle anymore. It feels like I’m crawling around inside my own skin, if that makes sense. Like I should be sitting down, I’m tired, I know I’m tired, but something in me is pushing me to get up and do the next thing.

And then I start doing one thing, and it reminds me of another thing, and before I know it I’m up and moving again—sorry, I know that’s not really the point. The point is I feel worn out, but I still can’t sit still inside. It’s been really upsetting.
Have you started or changed the dose of any medications recently, especially any antipsychotic or anti-nausea drugs?

I don’t think so… I mean, I’d have to look at the bottles because I keep them all in that cabinet, and then sometimes I move them to the kitchen so I remember, but then I forget why they’re there. 

But as far as I know, no one recently started me on anything like that or changed a dose. What kinds of nausea medicines do you mean?

When you feel this need to keep moving, do you also notice a lot of worrying or anxious thoughts running through your mind, or is it more just a physical urge to move without particular worries attached?

It’s more like… I can’t settle. I mean, I do get upset about it because it’s exhausting, but it feels like it starts in my body, like I’m crawling out of my own skin and I have to get up and do the next thing.

Even when I know I should be sitting still—like watching a show, or just resting—I feel worn out but still pushed to move. Then I’ll stand up and think, “Oh, I should do that,” and then another thing. But it’s not always that I’m worrying about one specific thing, if that’s what you mean. It’s just this inside restlessness.
Are you currently taking any medications at all, even ones you've been on for a while, especially anything for nausea, mood, or psychiatric symptoms?

I’m… honestly, I’m not completely sure off the top of my head. I have a couple bottles at home, but I’d need to look at them because I don’t keep it straight in my head—sometimes I put them by the sink, then I move them, and then I get annoyed because I can’t find what I just moved.

I don’t think there’s anything new for nausea or mood, though. Nothing that jumps out to me like that. But I’d probably have to bring the bottles in or write them down, because if I try to list them from memory I’m afraid I’ll get it wrong.
When you get up and move around or pace, does that actually make the restless feeling inside you better, even temporarily, or does it stay the same no matter what you do?

A little, maybe… but not really enough. Like, I get up because I feel like I can’t stay inside my own skin, if that makes sense, like I have to jump up and do the next thing even when I’m worn out.

Sometimes pacing sort of takes the edge off for a minute, but then I’m right back to feeling unsettled. I’ll sit down and it’s like, no, I can’t do this, I have to get up again. It’s exhausting.

Are you currently taking, or have you recently taken, any antipsychotic medications—such as risperidone, olanzapine, haloperidol, or aripiprazole—or any other drugs your doctor described as being for psychosis, mood stabilization, or severe agitation?

I don’t think so… those names don’t sound familiar to me, but I’m not great at keeping track of medication names. My daughter always says I should write them down in one place, and then I do, and then I can’t remember where I put the paper.

I don’t remember anyone saying “for psychosis” or anything like that. Mood stabilization… I’m not sure what would count. I’d have to check the bottles or ask the pharmacy, honestly.

Is this restless feeling mainly in your legs, and does it tend to get worse in the evening or at night when you're lying down, or does it happen all over your body throughout the day regardless of the time?

It’s not just my legs, no. I mean, my legs do get going because I’m up and down so much, but it feels more like my whole body, like I can’t settle inside my own skin anymore.

It can happen during the day too, not only when I’m lying down at night. I’ll be sitting there thinking I should rest, and then suddenly I have to jump up and do the next thing, even if I’m worn out. Like yesterday I was trying to sit after doing some dishes, and then I remembered something in the other room, and then I’m up again—so it’s not really just an evening thing.
Have you ever taken medications like metoclopramide (Reglan), prochlorperazine (Compazine), or promethazine for nausea, dizziness, or stomach issues—either recently or in the past?

I’m not sure. Reglan sounds maybe familiar, but I couldn’t tell you if that was me or someone else in the family. We’ve had so many little bottles around over the years, and my husband used to keep his in the kitchen drawer, which drove me crazy because then I’d put coupons in there and everything would get mixed up.

For nausea… I mean, I’ve had things prescribed here and there, but I don’t remember those names specifically. I’d probably need to look at the pharmacy list to be sure.
Roughly how long have you been experiencing this restless, can't-settle feeling—has it been going on for months to years, or did it start more recently, within the past few weeks?

It’s been… not just a few weeks, no. It really started causing me trouble after my husband died, and that was about a year and ten months ago now.

I mean, time gets funny after something like that—I still think of things like, “Oh, he’d know where that bill folder is,” and then I remember all over again. But yes, the not being able to settle, that’s been a real problem since then.
Since this started after your husband passed, have you also been feeling persistently sad, down, or preoccupied with thoughts about him and the loss, more so than just the physical restlessness?

I don’t know how to separate that exactly. I mean, I think about him, of course I do. Little things set it off—like I’ll see his mug, or I’ll go to tell him something and then remember he’s not there.

But whether that’s “persistently sad” in the way you mean… I’m not sure. Some days I’m just busy running around and then it hits me, and other times I’m more irritated that I can’t get anything done. It all kind of tangles together, if that makes sense.
Aside from thoughts about your husband, do you find yourself worrying a lot about other things—like your health, finances, or family—more days than not?

I mean… I worry, sure, but I don’t know if it’s “more days than not” in the way you’re asking. Some days it’s the bills, or I’ll wonder if I forgot to mail something, and then I’ll go looking for the envelope and end up cleaning out a drawer for twenty minutes.

But I wouldn’t say I’ve been keeping track of it. It’s hard to tell what’s normal worrying and what’s… whatever this is. My daughter tells me I overthink things, but she says that about the way I load the dishwasher too, so I don’t know.

When you're distracted by something enjoyable—like visiting with your daughter or watching a favorite show—does the restless, need-to-move feeling ease up at all, or does it stay just as strong no matter what you're doing or how you're feeling emotionally?

It’s… it’s like it’s there under everything. Even if I’m watching something I like, I still feel like I should get up and do the next thing. Like I can’t settle inside my own skin, if that makes sense.

I’ll sit down because I’m tired, and then two minutes later I’m thinking, no, I need to go check that, or move that, or start something else. Even when I’m worn out, I don’t feel still inside. Visiting with my daughter can distract me a bit, I suppose, but it doesn’t really turn it off.
Besides the restlessness, have you noticed muscle tension, trouble concentrating, or feeling on edge that seems to go along with it?

The concentrating part, yes. I’ll try to read something simple, like the senior center newsletter or the choir schedule, and I start out fine, you know, thinking I’m paying attention.

Then a few minutes later I realize my eyes have gone over the same lines three times and I couldn’t tell you what I just read. And then I’ll notice some little notice about the bake sale or who’s bringing coffee, and that reminds me I meant to call someone, and then I’ve lost the whole thing. So yes, concentrating has been hard.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past or recent use of specific nausea/dizziness/stomach medications, which is not covered by any symptom profile item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. Reglan sounds maybe familiar, but I couldn’t tell you if that was me or someone else in the family. We’ve had so many little bottles around over the years, and my husband used to keep his in the kitchen drawer, which drove me crazy because then I’d put coupons in there and everything would get mixed up.

For nausea… I mean, I’ve had things prescribed here and there, but I don’t remember those names specifically. I’d probably need to look at the pharmacy list to be sure.

inference.note: No new information confirmed or ruled out causative medication exposure; symptoms remain consistent with akathisia (drug-induced or unspecified) versus restless legs syndrome, though whole-body, non-circadian pattern makes RLS less likely. Maintaining both pending medication history clarification.

doctor.intent: Determine chronicity/onset pattern to distinguish long-standing RLS from a more recent drug-induced akathisia
doctor.question: Roughly how long have you been experiencing this restless, can't-settle feeling—has it been going on for months to years, or did it start more recently, within the past few weeks?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been causing real trouble since my husband died about 1 year and 10 months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the restless, can't-settle feeling has been going on, which directly matches the duration item.

patient.answer:
It’s been… not just a few weeks, no. It really started causing me trouble after my husband died, and that was about a year and ten months ago now.

I mean, time gets funny after something like that—I still think of things like, “Oh, he’d know where that bill folder is,” and then I remember all over again. But yes, the not being able to settle, that’s been a real problem since then.

inference.note: Symptoms are whole-body, occur throughout the day, and are not confined to the legs or worse at night, arguing against restless legs syndrome (G25.81), so it is removed. No clear antipsychotic/antiemetic exposure has been confirmed, so drug-induced akathisia (G25.71) remains only tentatively supported pending medication review. The temporal onset tightly linked to bereavement ~22 months ago raises consideration of an adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.21) or generalized anxiety with psychomotor restlessness (F41.1) as alternative explanations for the inner restlessness.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the restlessness is accompanied by depressive or grief-related symptoms (e.g., persistent sadness, preoccupation with the loss, guilt) that would support an adjustment disorder related to her husband's death, versus a primarily anxious or purely motor symptom pattern.
doctor.question: Since this started after your husband passed, have you also been feeling persistently sad, down, or preoccupied with thoughts about him and the loss, more so than just the physical restlessness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent sadness, low mood, or grief-related preoccupation after the husband’s death, which is not covered by the listed ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know how to separate that exactly. I mean, I think about him, of course I do. Little things set it off—like I’ll see his mug, or I’ll go to tell him something and then remember he’s not there.

But whether that’s “persistently sad” in the way you mean… I’m not sure. Some days I’m just busy running around and then it hits me, and other times I’m more irritated that I can’t get anything done. It all kind of tangles together, if that makes sense.

inference.note: No clear history of antipsychotic/antiemetic exposure, making akathisia less likely but not fully ruled out. Onset tightly linked to bereavement (~22 months ago) and description of restlessness as body-based rather than worry-driven keeps grief-related adjustment reaction and GAD as leading considerations.

doctor.intent: Determine whether she experiences excessive, wide-ranging worry (about health, finances, family, etc.) beyond the loss itself, which would suggest generalized anxiety disorder rather than an adjustment reaction tied specifically to the bereavement.
doctor.question: Aside from thoughts about your husband, do you find yourself worrying a lot about other things—like your health, finances, or family—more days than not?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about generalized worry/anxiety about health, finances, or family, which is not covered by the provided ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I mean… I worry, sure, but I don’t know if it’s “more days than not” in the way you’re asking. Some days it’s the bills, or I’ll wonder if I forgot to mail something, and then I’ll go looking for the envelope and end up cleaning out a drawer for twenty minutes.

But I wouldn’t say I’ve been keeping track of it. It’s hard to tell what’s normal worrying and what’s… whatever this is. My daughter tells me I overthink things, but she says that about the way I load the dishwasher too, so I don’t know.

inference.note: Reduced likelihood of GAD (F41.1) since patient denies persistent, pervasive worry more days than not, and worry seems situational rather than generalized. Akathisia (G25.71) remains possible pending confirmation of any antiemetic/antipsychotic exposure, but no clear medication link established yet. Symptom onset tightly tied to bereavement (~22 months ago) supports an adjustment/grief-related process (F43.21) with prominent psychomotor restlessness rather than primary anxiety disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is tied to emotional/psychological triggers (supporting adjustment disorder) or persists regardless of mood and distraction (supporting drug-induced akathisia)
doctor.question: When you're distracted by something enjoyable—like visiting with your daughter or watching a favorite show—does the restless, need-to-move feeling ease up at all, or does it stay just as strong no matter what you're doing or how you're feeling emotionally?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore, like I have to jump up and do the next thing even when I am worn out and should be sitting still.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the restless, need-to-move feeling changes with distraction or emotional state, which corresponds to the patient's restlessness symptom.

patient.answer:
It’s… it’s like it’s there under everything. Even if I’m watching something I like, I still feel like I should get up and do the next thing. Like I can’t settle inside my own skin, if that makes sense.

I’ll sit down because I’m tired, and then two minutes later I’m thinking, no, I need to go check that, or move that, or start something else. Even when I’m worn out, I don’t feel still inside. Visiting with my daughter can distract me a bit, I suppose, but it doesn’t really turn it off.

inference.note: Restlessness is persistent, whole-body, unrelieved by distraction, and temporally linked to bereavement rather than clearly to any antipsychotic or antiemetic exposure (patient denies these, though medication history remains uncertain). This keeps drug-induced akathisia (G25.71) as a possibility pending medication reconciliation, while the chronicity, lack of clear worry focus, and prominent psychomotor restlessness raise consideration of an anxiety-spectrum process (F41.1) alongside the grief-related adjustment reaction (F43.21).

doctor.intent: Assess whether the restlessness is accompanied by other core GAD symptoms (muscle tension, fatigue, concentration problems, irritability) that would support a generalized anxiety diagnosis rather than a purely motor phenomenon like akathisia or a grief-related adjustment reaction.
doctor.question: Besides the restlessness, have you noticed muscle tension, trouble concentrating, or feeling on edge that seems to go along with it?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I can sit down with the senior center newsletter or a choir schedule and start out fine, but after a few minutes I realize my eyes have gone over the same lines and I have no idea what I just read.
target_item.reason: The doctor asks about trouble concentrating along with restlessness; this item directly covers difficulty sustaining attention/concentration.

patient.answer:
The concentrating part, yes. I’ll try to read something simple, like the senior center newsletter or the choir schedule, and I start out fine, you know, thinking I’m paying attention.

Then a few minutes later I realize my eyes have gone over the same lines three times and I couldn’t tell you what I just read. And then I’ll notice some little notice about the bake sale or who’s bringing coffee, and that reminds me I meant to call someone, and then I’ve lost the whole thing. So yes, concentrating has been hard.

inference.note: Restlessness is whole-body, present throughout the day regardless of activity or distraction, and not confined to legs or worsened at rest/evening, arguing against akathisia (G25.71) or RLS. No confirmed exposure to antipsychotics or antiemetics further reduces likelihood of drug-induced akathisia. Symptoms have persisted nearly 2 years since bereavement, exceeding the typical 6-month window for adjustment disorder (F43.21), and are accompanied by chronic worry, concentration difficulty, and subjective restlessness more consistent with generalized anxiety disorder.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the visit
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient describes a pervasive, almost daily sense of inner restlessness and inability to settle, accompanied by fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and subjective worry that has persisted for nearly two years since her husband's death. Extensive questioning ruled out recent initiation or dose change of antipsychotic or antiemetic medications, making drug-induced akathisia unlikely. The restlessness is generalized (not confined to legs, not worse at night), argues against restless legs syndrome. The chronicity (>6 months), multiple somatic/cognitive symptoms (restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration), and mild but persistent worry about daily tasks, without a full major depressive syndrome or PTSD-specific re-experiencing/avoidance symptoms, best fit Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1). The temporal link to bereavement suggests grief as a psychosocial trigger but the symptom profile does not meet criteria for prolonged grief disorder or persistent depressive disorder, as she denies persistent low mood and the focus is on generalized restlessness/worry rather than grief-specific preoccupation.
